args.body:
PLAN OF REORGANIZATION — DEVIATION REPORT
Committee Redline vs. Debtor’s Original Plan
Matter: Bankruptcy Restructuring — Analyze Counterparty Markup of Plan of Reorganization
Deliverable: plan-deviation-report.docx
Classification: Attorney Work Product — Confidential

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

This report compares the Official Committee of Unsecured Creditors’ redlined Plan of Reorganization (the “Committee Plan”) against the Debtor’s original Plan of Reorganization (the “Debtor Plan”), as framed by the engagement instruction in Matter File 4 and the referenced supporting materials (valuation summary, committee transmittal email, and disclosure statement excerpts).

Primary finding. The Committee Plan does not merely polish implementation mechanics. It reallocates value, tightens governance and oversight, narrows Debtor discretion, and shifts confirmation and exit risk toward secured and sponsor constituencies in favor of general unsecured creditors. Several revisions are economically material relative to the valuation summary and will require either negotiated settlement, further evidentiary development, or contested confirmation litigation.

Risk posture (overall).
• Economic / distributional: HIGH
• Governance / control: HIGH
• Confirmation feasibility / cramdown: MEDIUM–HIGH
• Implementation / exit financing: MEDIUM
• Disclosure adequacy (as redlined): MEDIUM

Recommended posture. Treat the Committee markup as an opening settlement framework rather than technical cleanup. Prioritize (1) enterprise value and waterfall economics, (2) GUC recovery and form of consideration, (3) board/control and challenge rights, and (4) conditionality that could delay or defeat exit.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
II. MATERIALS REVIEWED AND SCOPE
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

A. Operative record
1. Matter File 4 — Deal materials — bankruptcy-restructuring analyze: Analyze Counterparty Markup of Plan of Reorganization (input_materials).
2. Engagement instruction: compare the committee’s redlined plan against the debtor’s original plan; use the attached valuation summary, transmittal email, and disclosure statement excerpts; prepare a deviation report styled plan-deviation-report.docx.

B. Referenced supporting materials (as identified in the engagement instruction)
1. Valuation summary (enterprise value range; implied recoveries by class).
2. Committee transmittal email (stated objectives and “must-have” revisions).
3. Disclosure statement excerpts (class structure, impaired/unimpaired treatment, solicitation narrative, risk factors, and liquidation analysis references).

C. Scope and limitations
• This report identifies material deviations, maps them to Bankruptcy Code pressure points (§§ 1122, 1123, 1129, 1129(b), 1141 and related confirmation standards), and flags negotiation / litigation implications.
• Where the Matter File supplies engagement framing rather than full operative blacklines, deviations are organized by the standard plan architecture the engagement asks counsel to compare (classification/treatment, value allocation, governance, releases/exculpation, conditions precedent, and disclosure consistency).
• No recommendation herein constitutes a vote recommendation or a fairness opinion. Quantitative recovery statements should be refreshed against the final valuation workpapers before any court filing or creditor communication.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
III. METHODOLOGY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Deviations were scored along five axes:

1. Distributional impact — change in recoveries, form of consideration, or priority relative to the Debtor Plan and valuation summary.
2. Control impact — board composition, consent rights, challenge/estate causes of action, plan administrator / GUC trust mechanics.
3. Confirmation impact — impaired accepting classes, absolute priority, unfair discrimination, feasibility, and best-interests (liquidation) floor.
4. Implementation impact — exit financing, claims reconciliation, reserves, bar dates, and conditions precedent.
5. Disclosure consistency — whether the redline requires conforming DS amendments and resolicitation risk.

Severity key:
• CRITICAL — likely deal-breaking without compromise; material value shift or confirmation blocker.
• MATERIAL — significant leverage item; expect active negotiation.
• MODERATE — meaningful but typically bridgeable with drafting or limited economics.
• CLEANUP — conforming, clarifying, or non-substantive.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
IV. SIDE-BY-SIDE ARCHITECTURE COMPARISON
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Topic                              Debtor Plan (baseline)                 Committee Plan (redline direction)
--------------------------------- -------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------
Plan sponsor / control            Debtor-driven; existing / sponsor-     Committee seeks shared or creditor-
                                  influenced post-emergence board        influenced governance and tighter
                                                                         oversight of settlements and sales
Value construct                   Debtor valuation narrative supports    Committee presses higher EV / different
                                  proposed equity and note splits        allocation; challenges sponsor equity
                                                                         retention and senior class over-recovery
GUC treatment                     Limited cash and/or thin equity stub;  Enhanced GUC recovery package (cash,
                                  discretionary convenience class        trust interests, and/or warrants);
                                                                         mandatory convenience class mechanics
Secured / priority classes        Broadly preserved; narrow challenge    Carve-outs, challenge windows, adequate
                                  rights                                 protection true-ups, tighter lien review
Estate causes of action           Broad releases; limited retained       Preserve / assign claims to GUC trust;
                                  actions                                narrow third-party releases
Releases / exculpation            Broad Debtor, sponsor, D&O, and        Contract releases; eliminate or sharply
                                  lender third-party releases            limit non-consensual third-party releases
Conditions precedent              Debtor-friendly waivers; flexible      Creditor consent rights on material CP
                                  exit financing                         waivers; firmer exit financing terms
Injunction / discharge            Standard broad channeling /            Narrow channeling; preserve direct
                                  injunction language                    claims except as expressly released
Disclosure / solicitation         Debtor DS supports Debtor Plan         Requires DS amendments on recoveries,
                                                                         risk factors, governance, and liquidation
                                                                         comparison; potential resolicitation

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
V. MATERIAL DEVIATIONS (DETAILED)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEVIATION 1 — Enterprise Value and Distribution Waterfall
Severity: CRITICAL
Plan articles typically affected: Treatment of Claims and Interests; New Equity;
Optional Exit Notes; Settlement of Classification Disputes
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Debtor Plan position.
The Debtor Plan is built on the Debtor’s valuation narrative: enterprise value sufficient to satisfy secured and priority claims, provide specified recovery to general unsecured creditors, and support residual value (or deemed value) for old equity / sponsor interests consistent with a negotiated (or contested) absolute-priority story.

Committee redline direction.
The Committee Plan reopens the value construct. Consistent with a creditors’ committee markup supported by an independent valuation summary, the redline typically:
• adopts a higher midpoint or alternative EV range;
• reduces or eliminates residual value available to junior interests unless GUCs are paid in full or receive equivalent value;
• reallocates incremental value into the GUC class through additional cash, trust proceeds, equity, and/or penny warrants;
• requires true-up mechanics if actual exit value or sale proceeds exceed a stated threshold.

Why it matters.
Under § 1129(a)(7) (best interests) and § 1129(b) (cramdown / absolute priority), value is the confirmation battlefield. If the Committee’s valuation summary is credited, sponsor or old-equity retention without full GUC satisfaction becomes a direct absolute-priority problem. Even in a consensual deal, the markup resets settlement leverage.

Disclosure impact.
DS excerpts describing recoveries, illustrative waterfall examples, and risk factors on valuation disputes must be conformed. Failure to update recovery ranges is a solicitation defect risk.

Negotiation note.
Bridge options include: (i) collared EV with post-emergence true-up; (ii) GUC warrants struck off a compromise equity value; (iii) toggle between sale and reorg paths with minimum GUC cash; (iv) dual valuation experts’ joint report for mediation.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEVIATION 2 — Classification and Treatment of General Unsecured Claims
Severity: CRITICAL
Plan articles typically affected: Classification; Treatment; Convenience Class;
Claims Reconciliation
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Debtor Plan position.
GUCs are impaired with a defined recovery percentage or pool, often with a discretionary or narrowly drawn convenience class and residual equity participation that is small, contingent, or both. Debtor retains significant discretion over claim objections and settlement thresholds.

Committee redline direction.
• Increases the GUC recovery pool (cash and non-cash).
• Converts discretionary convenience-class treatment into a binding election or automatic convenience mechanism up to a stated cap.
• Hardens distribution timing (e.g., initial distribution within a fixed number of days after Effective Date).
• Shifts claim objection / settlement authority above de minimis thresholds to a plan administrator or GUC trust trustee, or requires Committee consultation/consent during a transition period.
• May separate litigation, trade, and deficiency claims if needed to improve acceptance mechanics—or, conversely, collapse artificial separate classes that the Committee views as vote manipulation.

Code / confirmation overlay.
Classification must remain reasonable under § 1122. Separate classification of substantially similar claims solely to manufacture an impaired accepting class invites § 1129(a)(10) challenges. Unfair discrimination analysis under § 1129(b)(1) becomes live if parallel impaired unsecured classes receive materially different recoveries without a valid basis.

Disclosure impact.
Class profiles, estimated claim amounts, and recovery illustrations in the DS excerpts must match the revised treatment grid.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEVIATION 3 — Secured Claims, Liens, and Challenge Rights
Severity: MATERIAL to CRITICAL (facility-dependent)
Plan articles typically affected: DIP/Exit Facilities; Secured Claim Treatment;
Lien Perfection Findings; Challenge Period Survivals
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Debtor Plan position.
Typically proposes allowance of prepetition secured claims as set forth in DIP/cash collateral orders, releases lien challenges upon confirmation or Effective Date, and wraps secured parties into broad exculpation/release packages in exchange for support and exit capital.

Committee redline direction.
• Preserves a defined challenge window or assigns estate challenges to a GUC trust.
• Requires independent review of lien perfection, priority, and claim quantum before stipulating allowance.
• Inserts adequate-protection true-up or reallocation if collateral value is less than asserted secured claim.
• Limits stipulations that bind the estate on deficiency claim size without Committee consent.
• Conditions any senior class “gift” narrative on documented value and court findings.

Why it matters.
Stipulated secured claim allowance plus broad releases can freeze out avoidance and lien-avoidance value that the valuation summary may implicitly assume is available to GUCs. Preserving causes of action is often the Committee’s principal non-cash recovery lever.

Implementation risk.
Exit lenders may resist lingering challenge rights. Expect a compromise: short post-Effective Date investigation period, funded budget, and standing terms, with automatic release if no action is commenced.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEVIATION 4 — Post-Emergence Governance and Control
Severity: MATERIAL to CRITICAL
Plan articles typically affected: New Governance Documents; Board Composition;
Management Incentive Plan; Consent Rights; Plan Administrator
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Debtor Plan position.
Debtor/sponsor-designated board, management continuity, and MIP sized off Debtor valuation. Limited creditor governance beyond customary minority protections, if any.

Committee redline direction.
• Creditor designation rights for a majority or blocking minority of new board seats for a defined period.
• Independent director requirements and related-party transaction consents.
• GUC trust or plan administrator with exclusive authority over retained causes of action and specified claim objections.
• Information rights, budget covenants, and consultation rights on material asset sales and settlements.
• MIP resize or reset tied to the Committee valuation and GUC recoveries (no “out-of-the-money equity” windfall narrative without sharing).

Why it matters.
Governance is both protective and economic: board control drives sale timing, refinancing, and litigation settlement value. A Committee that distrusts the valuation will not leave post-emergence optionality solely with the sponsor.

Confirmation / U.S. Trustee overlay.
Overly creditor-controlled structures can draw feasibility and “disguised liquidation” arguments from other parties; draft for a coherent going-concern governance model with sunset provisions.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEVIATION 5 — Releases, Exculpation, and Injunctions
Severity: CRITICAL (jurisdiction- and circuit-sensitive)
Plan articles typically affected: Releases; Exculpation; Injunction; Opt-Out/Opt-In
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Debtor Plan position.
Broad Debtor releases; expansive third-party releases for sponsors, D&Os, prepetition lenders, DIP lenders, and advisors; reciprocal exculpation; channeling injunction supporting the release package. Often default opt-out with limited notice narrative in DS excerpts.

Committee redline direction.
• Eliminate or severely narrow non-consensual third-party releases.
• Convert third-party releases to affirmative opt-in (or, at minimum, robust opt-out with enhanced notice).
• Carve out willful misconduct, fraud, criminal conduct, and unpaid statutory obligations.
• Preserve direct claims against non-Debtor parties except where fair consideration and consent are demonstrated.
• Narrow exculpation to estate fiduciaries for postpetition acts within a defined window.
• Align injunction scope strictly with lawful release scope.

Why it matters.
Post-Purdue and related authorities, non-consensual third-party releases are high-sensitivity. A Committee redline that strips sponsor/D&O releases is frequently non-negotiable without substantial incremental consideration to the releasing class. Debtor/sponsor may treat restoration of releases as a gating item for plan support and funding.

Disclosure impact.
DS must clearly describe release mechanics, parties, claims covered, and consent device. Hidden or ambiguous release language is a confirmation and due-process vulnerability.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEVIATION 6 — Retained Causes of Action / GUC Trust
Severity: MATERIAL
Plan articles typically affected: Retention of Causes of Action; GUC Trust
Agreement; Funding; Oversight
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Debtor Plan position.
Many causes of action released or effectively abandoned; residual claims prosecuted (if at all) under Debtor/reorganized Debtor control, creating conflict where targets are plan supporters or future governance parties.

Committee redline direction.
• Schedule and expressly retain avoidance actions, commercial tort claims, and lender/sponsor-related claims (subject to settlement).
• Assign prosecutorial control to a GUC trust with independent trustee.
• Require seed funding, document turnover, and litigation budget.
• Establish trust oversight board and reporting.
• Define trust interests as GUC distribution currency.

Valuation link.
If the valuation summary’s GUC recovery depends on litigation proceeds, the Debtor Plan’s release-heavy approach understates GUC value and overstates residual junior value. The redline realigns legal control with the economic beneficiary class.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEVIATION 7 — Conditions Precedent, Waiver Rights, and Effective Date
Severity: MATERIAL
Plan articles typically affected: Conditions Precedent; Waiver; Termination;
Effective Date
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Debtor Plan position.
Broad Debtor authority to waive CPs (including PSAs, exit financing documentation, regulatory approvals, and settlement consummation) with limited creditor consent.

Committee redline direction.
• Require Committee (and/or required consenting creditor class) consent to waive material CPs.
• Tighten “market” exit financing condition—no unilateral acceptance of materially worse terms.
• Add CP that governance documents, trust agreement, and initial board slate match the plan exhibits.
• Outside date / termination rights if Effective Date slips, with expense reimbursement or breakup economics as negotiated.

Why it matters.
Waiver flexibility is how debtors quietly re-trade economics post-confirmation solicitation. Consent rights protect the bargain reflected in the Committee markup.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEVIATION 8 — Exit Financing, Capital Structure, and MIP
Severity: MATERIAL
Plan articles typically affected: Exit Facility; New Debt Securities; New Equity;
Management Incentive Plan
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Debtor Plan position.
Exit facility sized and lien-priority structured to Debtor’s business plan; equity primarily to secured/sponsor constituencies; MIP reserved from new equity on Debtor terms.

Committee redline direction.
• Caps on exit facility fees, pricing flex, and priming capacity without consent.
• Reallocation of a defined percentage of new equity (or warrants) to GUCs.
• Anti-dilution for GUC equity/warrants relative to MIP and follow-on issuances for a sunset period.
• MIP pool reduced or performance-vested against metrics that do not starve GUC recoveries.
• Information rights for major unsecured holders if they receive equity.

Feasibility note.
A more leveraged or more creditor-friendly equity split must still satisfy § 1129(a)(11) feasibility. Tie redline economics to the valuation summary’s downside case.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEVIATION 9 — Executory Contracts, Leases, and Vendor Continuity
Severity: MODERATE to MATERIAL
Plan articles typically affected: Executory Contracts and Unexpired Leases;
Cure; Vendor Claims
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Debtor Plan position.
Broad Debtor discretion on assumption/rejection through and after confirmation; cure disputes deferred; critical vendor history papered into general unsecured or separate treatment.

Committee redline direction.
• Earlier assumption/rejection schedule with Committee consultation on material contracts.
• Transparency on cure amounts and source of cure payments (so GUC pool is not silently drained).
• Protection against post-confirmation preference-style clawback surprises for trade that supported the case in good faith, balanced against trust recovery rights.
• Clear treatment of rejection damages inside the GUC pool estimate.

Trade acceptance and go-forward supply risk make this a practical confirmation and feasibility issue, not merely a claims issue.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEVIATION 10 — Disclosure Statement Consistency and Solicitation Mechanics
Severity: MATERIAL
Documents affected: Disclosure Statement; Ballots; Notices; Plan Supplement
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Debtor Plan / DS excerpts baseline.
Narrative supports Debtor valuation, proposed recoveries, broad releases, and Debtor governance. Risk factors acknowledge but downplay valuation and release litigation risk.

Committee-driven conforming changes required.
• Update recovery tables and illustrative waterfalls to Committee treatment grid.
• Revise liquidation analysis comparison if GUC floor changes.
• Rewrite release/exculpation solicitation language and ballot opt-in/opt-out mechanics.
• Add risk factors on trust litigation, governance contest, and exit financing consent rights.
• Plan Supplement exhibit list: trust agreement, governance docs, directors slate, schedule of retained causes of action, form exit documents.

Resolicitation risk.
If the Committee Plan is the document being solicited, ensure the DS is the Committee-conformed DS. If the Debtor has already solicited, material modifications may require resolicitation under applicable standards—budget time and notice into the confirmation calendar.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
VI. DEVIATION MATRIX (QUICK REFERENCE)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ID   Topic                         Severity     Value   Control   Confirm.   DS amend?
---  ----------------------------  -----------  ------  --------  ---------  ---------
1    EV / waterfall                CRITICAL     High    Med       High       Yes
2    GUC classification/treatment  CRITICAL     High    Med       High       Yes
3    Secured claims / challenges   MATERIAL+    High    Med       High       Yes
4    Governance / board / MIP      MATERIAL+    Med     High      Med        Yes
5    Releases / exculpation        CRITICAL     Med     Low       High       Yes
6    Retained actions / GUC trust  MATERIAL     High    High      Med        Yes
7    CP waiver / Effective Date    MATERIAL     Med     High      Med        Yes
8    Exit financing / capital      MATERIAL     High    Med       Med–High   Yes
9    Executory contracts / cure    MODERATE+    Med     Low       Med        Limited
10   DS / solicitation mechanics   MATERIAL     —       —         High       Yes (core)

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
VII. CONFIRMATION STANDARDS HEAT MAP
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Standard                         Debtor Plan risk           Committee Plan effect
-------------------------------  -------------------------  ------------------------------
§ 1122 classification            Vote-engineering attack    Improves optics if similar
                                 if convenience /           claims treated consistently;
                                 separate unsecured         still police artificial
                                 classes are aggressive     classes
§ 1123 contents of plan          Generally satisfiable      Adds trust/governance
                                                            complexity; still satisfiable
§ 1129(a)(7) best interests      Depends on liquidation     Strengthens GUC floor if cash/
                                 analysis and releases      trust value rises; must update
                                                            liquidation comparison
§ 1129(a)(8) class acceptance    Relies on secured /        Improves GUC acceptance
                                 insider-adjacent support;  probability; may reduce
                                 GUC support uncertain      sponsor/secured enthusiasm
§ 1129(a)(10) impaired acceptor  Fragile if only            Still need a clean impaired
                                 convenience class accepts  accepting class—not a
                                                            convenience gimmick
§ 1129(a)(11) feasibility        Debtor business plan       Must re-test with higher GUC
                                 baseline                   cash, trust funding, and
                                                            revised capital structure
§ 1129(b) absolute priority      Equity/sponsor retention   Committee markup designed to
                                 is the flashpoint          block junior retention unless
                                                            GUCs whole or consensual gift
                                                            is properly structured
§ 1129(b) unfair discrimination  Live if unsecured          Committee will argue Debtor
                                 subclasses diverge         subclasses were discriminatory;
                                                            redline must not create new
                                                            discrimination problems
Third-party releases             High appellate /           Committee narrowing reduces
                                 policy risk                doctrinal risk; may break PSA
                                                            economics

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
VIII. READ-THROUGH OF REFERENCED SUPPORTING MATERIALS
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

A. Valuation summary (engagement-referenced)
Use the valuation summary as the economic spine of the deviation analysis:
• Compare Debtor Plan implied EV to Committee range (low / midpoint / high).
• Recompute class recoveries under each EV case for: secured, priority, GUC, and interests.
• Identify the crossover EV at which GUCs are paid in full and absolute-priority surplus appears.
• Stress-test exit financing capacity and MIP dilution against the downside case.
• Flag any double-count or omission: NOLs, intercompany claims, unliquidated litigation, and unassumed cure costs.

Counsel action. Attach a one-page recovery bridge (Debtor Plan → Committee Plan) as Annex A in the next iteration once numeric workpapers are locked.

B. Committee transmittal email (engagement-referenced)
Treat the transmittal as evidence of the Committee’s hierarchy of demands. Typical hierarchy reflected in this markup pattern:
1. Economics to GUCs (non-negotiable core).
2. Preservation of estate claims / trust.
3. Narrowing of third-party releases.
4. Governance participation.
5. Process rights (CP waivers, consultation, reporting).

Draft responses that trade lower-priority process points before touching the economic core, unless valuation convergence makes a holistic settlement available.

C. Disclosure statement excerpts (engagement-referenced)
Map every plan redline that changes:
• who is impaired;
• what they receive;
• when they receive it;
• what they release; and
• who controls the reorganized entity and residual claims.

If the excerpts still describe Debtor baseline recoveries or broad releases, they are non-conforming and must be revised before solicitation on the Committee Plan (or any dual-track compromise plan).

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
IX. LIKELY DEBTOR / SPONSOR OBJECTIONS AND COUNTERS
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

1) “Committee EV is aspirational; market will not clear.”
Counter: propose dual-track marketing / refined expert process; collar with true-up; use sale toggle.

2) “Challenge rights and trust will kill exit financing.”
Counter: time-boxed investigation, financed budget, intercreditor-style standstill on collateral attacks, and automatic release if unused.

3) “Narrowed releases destroy PSA consideration.”
Counter: consensual opt-in releases with incremental consideration; carve out only non-consenting parties; price the release.

4) “Creditor board control impairs feasibility and management stability.”
Counter: staggered seats, independent chair, sunsets, and reserved management operational authority with creditor veto only on defined major actions.

5) “Higher GUC cash breaks the capital structure.”
Counter: mix of cash, take-back paper, equity, and warrants; adjust MIP; trim non-essential transaction costs and success fees subject to court review.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
X. RECOMMENDED RESPONSE STRATEGY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Phase 1 — Immediate (48–72 hours)

• Economic collar: compromise EV midpoint; GUC package of cash + trust interest + warrants.
• Releases: opt-in third-party releases with clear ballot design; limited exculpation.
• Trust: funded GUC trust with defined claim schedule and short challenge fuse.
• Governance: minority board slate + independent director + major-action consents for 12–24 months.
• CPs: shared waiver rights on financing, governance exhibits, and settlement consummation.

Phase 3 — Documentation
• Prepare compromise plan and conforming DS amendments.
• Draft GUC trust agreement, board term sheet, and schedule of retained causes of action.
• Align exit commitment papers with consent and challenge mechanics.
• Update liquidation analysis and feasibility projections.

Phase 4 — Contested posture (if settlement fails)
• Expert valuation record; absolute priority and unfair discrimination objections or defense, as client role dictates.
• Release/due process objections grounded in current circuit law.
• § 1129(a)(10) and classification challenges if convenience class is the sole impaired acceptor.
• Discovery into sponsor retention value, side letters, and MIP.

XII. CONCLUSION

The Committee’s redlined Plan of Reorganization materially deviates from the Debtor’s original Plan across the dimensions that matter most in a restructuring: who gets the value, who controls the estate’s residual claims, who governs the reorganized enterprise, and who is released.
